todayInHistory.title: Life Aboard the Edmund Fitzgerald Described in Letters from Cadet
todayInHistory.text: David "Cowboy" Weiss in 1974. [GLSHS] DETROIT, MI – It wasn't just the hat that earned Edmund Fitzgerald crew member David Weiss his nickname "Cowboy." It was his friend and Great Lakes Maritime Academy classmate David James, who had just watched Frank Zappa's 1971 movie "200 Motels" featuring the character Lonesome Cowboy Burt. When James saw Weiss standing outside a classroom dressed in black and wearing a cowboy hat, the nickname came easily."He looked a little different," James said. Weiss was less "bummy" than the rest of their classmates, who dressed to emulate the sailors they were training to join. The day they met, James gave Weiss his nickname "Cowboy Burt." DuMouchelles auction house in downtown Detroit is selling letters written by a man killed in the Edmund Fitzgerald sinking in Lake Superior on Nov. 10, 1975. The letters were written by David Weiss while he was on the Fitzgerald. The friendship between Weiss and James is chronicled in a series of letters they exchanged while out on the inland seas in 1975, when Weiss was on the Edmund Fitzgerald and James on the Walter A. Sterling. The last was sent Oct. 30, about two weeks before Weiss went down with the Edmund Fitzgerald during a storm in Lake Superior. Twenty-eight crewmates perished along with him. The letters Weiss sent James that year are up for auction at DuMouchelles auction house in downtown Detroit along with photos, a postcard and other memorabilia, such as a letter Weiss's mom wrote to James after We

todayInHistory.title: Maritime Historian Valerie van Heest to Speak In Ludington
todayInHistory.text: LUDINGTON, MI – Maritime historian, author and shipwreck explorer Valerie van Heest, whose work has helped shape the visitor experience at all three Mason County Historical Society museums, will be the featured speaker at the society’s annual dinner meeting Thursday, Dec. 3. Maritime Historian Valerie van Heest. [Mason County Historical Society] Van Heest, one of Michigan’s leading maritime historians and shipwreck researchers, will present “History of the Great Lakes,” based on her new book, “A History of the Great Lakes in Twelve Shipwrecks.” The program will explore 250 years of Great Lakes history through a dozen shipwrecks, showing how these underwater discoveries reveal broader stories of conflict, settlement, innovation and change. The annual meeting will take place at the United Methodist Church of Ludington, 5810 Bryant Road. Doors will open at 5:45 p.m., with dinner beginning at 6 p.m. The society’s annual business meeting and organizational updates will follow dinner, and van Heest’s presentation will begin at 7:30 p.m. Van Heest is co-founder and president of the Michigan Shipwreck Research Association and has helped discover about 20 shipwrecks off Michigan’s west coast while participating in archaeological investigations at more than 50 shipwreck sites throughout the Great Lakes. Her work combines archival research with underwater exploration, including side-scan sonar surveys, remotely operated vehicles and archaeological documentation. She has also spent years

marineWeather.synopsis: 30.3 inch high pressure over western Ontario slowly shifts southeast over the western half of Lake Superior today and expands towards the southern U.S. by Saturday. This high continues to shift southeast, expand, and build through the weekend, centered over the Ohio River Valley at 30.5 inches by Monday afternoon. On Wednesday a 29.6 inch low pressure will move from the Rockies to the Dakotas, with Lake Superior between this low and the high pressure centered over the Mid-Atlantic states at 30.4 inches.

No major changes to the going forecast this morning. Northerly winds will remain steadily breezy (though below gale thresholds) through today and into Saturday with high pressure of 30.4 inches positioned well to the northwest. Winds will taper Sunday into Monday as 30.5 inch high pressure builds directly over the open waters. Persistent northerly winds will allow for continued lake effect precipitation today. Low level temperatures will be supportive for mainly rain, though some snow could mix in over the northern half of the lake. A few thunderstorms are possible, particularly over the southern half of the waters. Can't rule out a waterspout in any deeper thunderstorms that manage to develop.

Northerly flow will hold through Saturday which will support breezy conditions along with lake effect precipitation across Lake Huron. High pressure, 30.40 inches, to build in over the southern Great Lakes Sunday into Monday, producing quieter weather.

A trough averaging 29.80 inches will persist over the eastern Great Lakes through Saturday before shifting east on Sunday. High pressure 30.40 inches will build east over the region late Sunday through much of the week.

A trough averaging 29.9 inches will linger over the lake through Saturday night as its parent coastal low of 29.3 inches wobbles northeastward from near Nantucket to near Newfoundland. Sunday through Tuesday, a ridge averaging 30.5 inches will build from the Upper Midwest to the mid-Atlantic States.
